**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (299 words):**

Crypto prices on the Web are quoted in dollars, but not every exchange's dollar is worth a dollar. Some exchanges quote in stablecoins, others in balances on their own ledger, redeemable only through their banks. When the banks leave, that dollar drifts. Feeds and oracles average exchange prices as if all were in one dollar and report the drift as a price move or stablecoin failure. Separating the two is hard because an exchange's dollar is never quoted directly and any one asset may carry its own shock. We build on the law of one price and triangular arbitrage. Bitcoin has no peg, so its price gap between the troubled exchange and one with working banks measures the ledger's loss, and the rest of a stablecoin's move is the token's. We accept the split only if an unrelated asset shows the same gap, the implied token price matches its price elsewhere, and cross-rates hold. In banking cut-offs at three exchanges, 2017 to 2023, the exchange's dollar broke on Bitfinex and Binance.US but barely moved on Binance's sterling and euro rails, while in the March 2023 USD Coin run the method attributed the dislocation to the token. On Bitfinex the dollar fell by up to 844 basis points (bps), with bitcoin and ether agreeing to within 7.2 bps, and on both exchanges one episode swung from discount to premium before recovering. A multi-exchange bitcoin index was off by at least 100 bps for 2,826 hours; dropping exchange-hours our monitor flagged removed 88% of them. In 2018 the monitor flagged Bitfinex 3 days before its deposit freeze was reported, 6.5 months before regulators disclosed its loss and 7 months before CoinMarketCap dropped it by hand. The results are descriptive and give price feeds a public, hourly test of whose dollar moved.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
